newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bildt steps down after rough ride as Bosnia envoy.
newsitem.headline: Bildt steps down after rough ride as Bosnia envoy.

text.p: International peace envoy Carl Bildt, like so many of his predecessors in the Balkans, will be leaving Bosnia without any clear successes but full of warnings about a perilous future.

Bildt, a former Swedish prime minister, is stepping down as the international High Representative to Bosnia. On Friday, the international community named former Spanish foreign minister Carlos Westendorp as his successor after Italy dropped initial objections to him.
Westendorp will take over on June 20, said diplomats who were in the Portuguese town of Sintra for a meeting of states overseeing the Dayton peace accords that ended the Bosnian war 18 months ago.

Since Bildt, 48, who says he plans to return to Swedish politics, arrived on the scene to oversee the civilian side of the peace agreement, Bosnia has not moved much closer to reconciliation or to a stable peace.
Rival nationalist leaders keep it divided by waging war through other means, sabotaging attempts to reverse the results of "ethnic cleansing" and territorial conquest.
Bildt's critics in Bosnia viewed him as the personification of an uncaring world, too ready to make compromises with hardline nationalists.
His aides say his hands were tied because the post lacked any real power and the United States preferred to launch its own initiatives without consulting Bildt or European powers.
From the outset, Bildt had limited authority and limited funds to carry out the Herculean task of pushing through the civilian aspects of the U.S.-brokered peace treaty.
He was forced to rely on moral suasion as his small staff tried to breathe life into a new central government comprised of wartime enemies.

Bildt suffered his worst setback soon after assuming his post when Serb-held suburbs around Sarajevo were handed over to the Moslem-Croat federation amid an orgy of looting, arson and a mass exodus of Serb residents.
"That was a low moment. The handover of the suburbs was a great disappointment." said one aide.

Bildt was heavily criticised for extending a deadline for the departure of Serb police from the suburbs. In the days leading up to the handover, Serb authorities destroyed property and sowed terror among the Serbs who tried to stay.
As he tried to build international consensus, Bildt was caught in power struggles between Washington and Europe, Western and Islamic countries and European Union states.
Bosnian Moslem leaders viewed Bildt with suspicion, partly because of his friendly ties to the former Conservative government in Britain which opposed Western military intervention during the war.
With his spectacles and grasp of detail, Bildt sometimes resembled a youthful university professor trying to educate the world about the peace treaty.
It was the hardline Bosnian Serb leadership, and particularly indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic, who irritated the usually unflappable Bildt.

Last May, Bildt promoted a pragmatic rival to Karadzic but the intiative failed miserably. Bildt's announcement that he had succeeded in securing the end of the Karadzic era turned out to be premature.
It was not until U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke, the architect of the Dayton peace treaty, stepped in that Karadzic at last quit public office under heavy international pressure.

Bildt's work as a soldier for the international community has enhanced his personal popularity back home. He is returning to Swedish politics to try to unify opposition parties into a successful coalition.

Although Bildt has spoken of "minor miracles" achieved during his term, he issued stern warnings before his departure. Bildt said war could erupt again unless indicted war criminals are brought to justice and NATO peacekeeping troops extend their mission beyond a mid-1998 deadline.
